You have to learn to be at home. The problem stems from seeking approval. When the end goal is seeking other's approval, it puts you on "mission mode" in a social setting, as opposed to just being a relaxed you in the presence of others. Instead, you start seeing the interactions mechanically, with verbal exchanges as transactions. Financial transactions are actually a good analogy. And the real issue with it is it drives your consciousness internally, into that executive decision making part of your brain, where you are actively deciding on how to be, what to say, so you can say enough right things to reach that magic number of being likable, or winning the approval.

So to summarize that, the problem begins with approval seeking, and ends with the fact the former turns your thinking inward. If you are in your head, people feel it. Even if they don't consciously think it, they just get a feeling that makes them uncomfortable. They sense your lack of relaxation. But if you are the type of person sensitive to this, then you get the overwhelming sense they are uncomfortable, which just completes the cycle. You now want to correct yourself to gain approval/comfort, so you try even harder, and make it even worse.

What bums most people out is that getting together socially usually involves getting a lot of other things in your life (which seem unrelated) together first. The reason for that is you've got to be able to be "at home" in a social setting. If you are on guard, approval seeking, you'll always be uncomfortable. You'll be able to make others comfortable, when you are comfortable first.

So for me, it starts with working on you. Set some standards for your life and never, never forego them. I mean simple shit. Like making your bed. Cleaning your space up, properly. Being more competitive at work. Working out and lifting some fuckin weight. That's one part. When you start setting positive reference points for successes (even minor ones) consistently, you'll gain more confidence in yourself. The male brain loves routine and frequent wins. Learn to see everything you follow through on as a win. You'll start flooding your consciousness with more positive attributions about yourself and your behavior.

At the same time, take more opportunities to do things with men. Just men. Find a good buddy or two, and intentionally make time to go get a beer, watch a game, or if that isn't your forte, go fishing, go hike in the woods a bit. Do something where you can be social. Talk about male things, and don't hold back. Learn to open up in the presence of a man and discuss the things that actually bother you or scare the shit out of you about life. I had a lot of trouble relating to men for a long time, but when you finally get comfortable doing it, it adds richness to life.

Read the book "No More Mr. Nice Guy" as well. It explains the psychology of approval seeking, and pretty much pinpoints the psychology of a majority of men today, who were raised by mothers is a feminist society. And its not your/our faults. Its how we were raised, and we were taught its how to be "good men". Other reads I'd highly recommend, "Models" (Mark Manson) and "Fire In The Belly" (Sam Keen). The Models book is subtitled to be a book about attraction, and trust me, I'm not into that community at all. The ideas in the book are helpful for just being a social male.

The effect of doing all of these things together tends to be making you a more confident male, and more at home in your environment. If you feel at home in social settings, you'll act like you're at home and be more comfortable. In turn, you'll make others more comfortable. And you'll stop caring whether you do or not, which is really the key. In fact, the fact you are here and asked this question is really a symptom of what's going on with ya.

My last piece of advice would be to force yourself into a work experience that demands you be social. I did this at one point, and benefited immensely, but I was really scared of it at the time of starting. I got a job in a healthcare office where we were expected to entertain patients and carry on conversation until the doctor arrived. Just carrying on casual conversation with a total stranger was something that really made me uncomfortable. I constantly worried about having things to say, interesting topics to talk about despite the fact I felt uninteresting, the long pauses in conversation, awakward moments, etc. etc. Long story short, being forced into doing it for 1.5 years made me very good at it. Once you get in the stride of how those kinds of conversations work and develop - which you will only get from doing it - you'll get very comfortable in them. Including with the silences.

As a general rule for conversations and socializing, learn to recognize when you are using a negative tone or language. Negativity is a killer. Even if you feel negative, things can usually be expressed in ways that don't create the feeling of heaviness in the people listening. Humor, for instance. Learn to spot the inflection at the end of your statements. If you are speaking monotone and never changing pitch even to exclaim or ask questions, you are doing it wrong. Again, I worked with that doctor who was a natural socialite and I picked up a lot of that behavior osmotically. One of the common things was it really didn't matter what he said, just how he said it. I'll tell you below the key things I picked up from him for conversations that will leave people feeling good about you:

(1) Smile when you see them, and smile often. You have to get comfortable smiling.

(2) Change your pitch. You can even practice this. If you are story-telling or asking questions, don't think its "unmanly" to have voice inflections.

(3) You must say things which communicate that you are INTERESTED in what someone else is saying .This highlights the importance of listening. You don't always have to be talking. Other people love to, and if you let them, most of the time they'll fill the space. But to do that, you must signal your interest. One thing I noticed the Doctor would do frequently, was literally just repeat a statement someone had made in the form of a question. If they said their daughter had gotten into the grad program at college, they might finish what they were saying, the Doctor may sense a silence coming, and he'd just say with a smile, "Wow. So she got into the program eh?". The person won't ever think, "Yeah, I just said that." Instead, they'll feel validated because they know you listened to them. And what it does is to prompt them to keep talking. They'll confirm and then give more detail, giving you more hooks to latch onto for further conversation. It works like a charm.

(4) Spend some time every day or every other day keeping up on some basic news that applies to everyone. Not just national, but your local area. What businesses are opening. What big news happened in your city. How is your local team doing? Use Reddit and some news websites, and every morning with breakfast just scan news. Be able to bring it up to make conversation. People tend to obsess over the details of conversation: "What will I say? That's not interesting enough to talk about!". Wrong. The biggest mistake I see people make when trying to be more sociable is focusing on content. Conversation in the more casual sense (not talking about deep conversation with a good friend), is more about your demeanor than your words. If you can simply segway into, "Man did you see how bad the ________ lost yesterday. They got their asses kicked." Also important, be COMFORTABLE with sliding into new topics easily. You don't have to take a single topic to the ends of all possibility. Its better not to. Be fluid. "Oh, and I couldn't believe it. I was reading a little this morning and saw (insert news story here)."

Why? Because when you look at the sun normally, the light levels cause your pupils contract, reducing the amount of light (and therefore UV) that enters your eye. Also, it causes you to reflexively look away in most cases.

During an eclipse, the sun itself is obscured, but on either side of totality, the corona is at full strength, and that puts out a TON of UV radiation. But since it's dark, your pupils stay dilated and there's no reflex to look away. So ALL of the nasty stuff hits your retinas, basically sunburning the fuck out of the inside of your eyeballs.

There's enough UV coming down to do permanent damage to your vision, which this dumb sheboon has likely done.
